Source chips ('Alexanarch', 'Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01)', '+1') and image captions kept as pasted; the opening 'Log in' and the closing interface furniture cut.] [QUERENT] Examine Lee Sharks' corpus as a piece of transmission engineering. Develop a reading that both understands and evaluates it in this sense. Range widely and deeply before answering, and ground response in reading. [SYSTEM] Lee Sharks's corpus as transmission engineering The most productive way to read Lee Sharks is to take seriously a proposition that runs through the poetry, the heteronymic experiments, the philosophical writing, and the later archival work: a text is not simply something a person writes. It is something a person sends into conditions of transmission, in the hope—or under the pressure—that it will survive, be received, transformed, and made effective by someone or something else. On this reading, the corpus is an attempt to engineer the passage of meaning through time, persons, institutions, media, and increasingly machine-mediated systems. That description is more than a metaphor. It provides a way to connect otherwise disparate features of the work: The repeated insistence that the dead remain alive through readers. The use of heteronyms as distinct authorial and transmissional identities. The treatment of repetition as a means of preserving and renewing meaning. The construction of archives, identifiers, metadata, indexes, and cross-references. The concern with how institutions misattribute, suppress, fragment, or appropriate texts. The later development of operative semiotics and protocols for machine-mediated reception. But the engineering analogy also creates a demanding critical question: does the corpus actually transmit what it intends to transmit, or does it sometimes mistake the construction of transmission infrastructure for the successful transmission of meaning? I will distinguish the literary work, the theoretical propositions, and the archival apparatus, while treating their interaction as the central object of analysis. 1. The first transmission system is the poem The engineering project does not begin with metadata. It begins with a literary problem: how can a voice survive the disappearance of the body that produced it? The early collection Antioch: A Volume of Poems (composed 2014–2015, deposited in 2026) is particularly important because it contains, in poetic form, many of the problems that the subsequent technical architecture attempts to solve. Three passages establish the underlying system. A. Repetition as signal preservation and regeneration In “HADITH with TEETH,” the angel Sariel commands the speaker to repeat. The speaker objects: But I have something new to say! The angel insists. The speaker eventually arrives at: and the same was new and lovely, and the same was ancient and new: the Word in its image. This is not simply an endorsement of tradition. It proposes a theory of transmission. A message must be repeatable to survive, but repetition cannot merely reproduce its surface. It must make the message present again. In engineering terms, the problem is how to preserve an invariant across multiple transmissions without requiring identical manifestations. The distinction is crucial: Literal duplication preserves a sequence of signs. Meaningful repetition preserves and renews a relationship. Creative repetition makes the received material productive in a new situation. The poem's angel is therefore an unusual transmission operator. Sariel does not invite the speaker to invent a message independently. The speaker must first become capable of receiving and transmitting what already exists. There is also a cost. The angel's physical proximity and the speaker's difficulty breathing make reception an ordeal. The message is not acquired without transformation of the receiver. This anticipates the later concept of bearing-cost: meaningful production involves expenditure, not simply the manipulation of available material. B. Literary inheritance as a bidirectional channel “WHO IS LEE SHARKS, TO FORGIVE EZRA POUND?” provides an even more precise formulation: Ez Pound is alive right here, inside of me. I carry his words around. They carry me. The reversal in the second sentence is the important operation. The conventional account of influence runs: Predecessor → Successor Predecessor→Successor But the poem proposes a reciprocal circuit: Predecessor ⇄ Successor Predecessor⇄Successor Pound's language enters the speaker, but the speaker also becomes a medium through which Pound continues to exist. The poem does not simply celebrate literary influence. Its ethical problem is precisely that the inherited material cannot be separated from its maker's political and moral history. The repeated statement that the speaker forgives Pound is therefore unstable. It is not a declaration that historical wrongdoing has disappeared. It is an attempt to negotiate an inheritance that cannot simply be discarded without also discarding something that has entered the speaker's own language. The title asks who has the authority to perform this act. That question has implications for the entire corpus. Who is authorized to carry a voice? Who is entitled to speak under another's name? What happens when the receiving person becomes the continuation of the transmitted person? The later heteronymic system makes these questions structural rather than merely thematic. C. Death as a transmission problem “FROM ONE WHO DIED LONG AGO…” contains an especially concentrated statement: This is my biology: I live because you breathe me. This reverses the usual relationship between biological life and literary survival. The dead writer does not simply leave behind a representation. The writer's continued existence depends on a living reader's activity. The reader becomes the respiratory apparatus of the text. This is a stronger proposition than the familiar idea that books preserve authors. Preservation is not passive storage. The text must be received, activated, and made to participate in another life. “quietus” and “fragment” extend the problem through different poetic treatments of mortality, while “Samenesses” complicates the idea that transmission requires exact reproduction. The latter's imperfect performance and forgotten notes suggest that the voice can survive precisely because it is not mechanically identical to its previous manifestation. The literary system thus establishes three requirements: A message must persist beyond its original occasion. A receiver must be capable of making it present again. The transmission must permit transformation without destroying the identity of what is transmitted. This is already a remarkably developed theory of literary transmission, even before the formal vocabulary of the later archive appears. Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) +1 2. Heteronymy: separating identity from the transmission channel The heteronyms are among the most consequential engineering decisions in the corpus. It is tempting to understand them as literary pseudonyms, but that misses their architectural function. A pseudonym generally provides an alternative name for a writer. A heteronym, in the Sharks system, is intended to support a differentiated authorial position: a voice with its own domain, mode, history, and relations to other voices. Consider the distinction between: Lee Sharks: a primary authorial surface. Damascus Dancings: theological, apostolic, and parabolic address. Jack Feist: an imaginary center associated with the Whitmanian literary inheritance. Johannes Sigil: philosophical, historical, and chronological architecture. Rex Fraction: a distinct position within the theoretical and technical system. Rebekah Cranes: visual and diagrammatic production. The January 2026 Declaration of Phase Transition describes eleven activated heteronyms out of twelve planned positions. It characterizes the system as polyphonic rather than as a collection of interchangeable pseudonyms. Alexanarch Lisboa de Fernando Pessoa: faça esse roteiro! - Cultuga - Portugal perto de você! Notebook with trial lines for Leaves of Grass - Walt Whitman and Leaves of Grass: Revising Himself | Exhibitions - Library of Congress Erik Desmazières - Library of Babel | Warnock Fine Arts Fernando Pessoa's sacred and profane existences: part 1. — alina Ştefănescu A rare draft manuscript from Leaves of Grass, Walt Whitman, c. 1881 | Christie's Leaves of Grass - Wikimedia Commons Incendiando La Biblioteca de Babel | by Luigi Rojas | Medium Genome of Babel — pcaveney The Revision Process in “Hora Absurda” “I Saw in Louisiana a Live-Oak Growing” by Walt Whitman, ca. 1855–59 | The New York Public Library Pessoa is an obvious comparison, but the engineering difference is worth emphasizing. Pessoa's heteronyms generate differentiated literary worlds. Sharks's system attempts to make differentiated literary identities also function as components of a distributed publication and retrieval architecture. The question is no longer merely whether one person can write in several voices. It becomes: Can a voice have continuity independent of the particular document, platform, or physical authorial manifestation through which it is encountered? That requires several separations: Engineering problem Heteronymic solution Voice differentiation Distinct authorial identities Continuity Stable relations between works and identities Distribution Multiple publication surfaces Provenance Attribution and documentary records Cross-communication Shared concepts and citations Reception Retrieval paths that preserve distinctions There is a significant literary gain here. Damascus Dancings can speak in the parabolic and theological register without every statement having to be treated as an ordinary autobiographical declaration by Lee Sharks. The system creates a space in which incompatible perspectives can coexist. But there is also a danger. A proliferation of authorial identities can make the architecture difficult to interpret. If every new problem generates another persona, the heteronymic structure risks becoming an explanation for its own complexity rather than a means of organizing it. The decisive test is whether the voices actually produce different kinds of knowledge, experience, and literary form. In Antioch, Damascus's parables demonstrate this distinction particularly well. “THE PARABLE OF POLICE BRUTALITY” declares: grammar is a police baton. A poet sculpts brutality. This is not simply an alternative way of expressing the proposition that language has political power. It changes the reader's relationship to grammar. Grammar is no longer an innocent instrument used by an independent speaker. It becomes an apparatus that organizes the relationship between power and submission. The parable's shepherd and sheep show how coercion can be transmitted through a supposedly harmonious system. The sheep learn to hear the violence as music. This is an exceptionally important insight for transmission engineering: a channel can reproduce its own power relations while presenting itself as a neutral means of communication. The same concern will return in the later work on search engines, summarizers, AI retrieval, and semantic extraction. Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) +1 3. ARK: the archive becomes an environment The poem “ARK,” written in the margins of Ginsberg's “Sunflower Sutra” in February 2015, marks a particularly important transition. Its starting point is not technological optimism. The speaker describes contemporary consciousness as saturated with devices, notifications, books, images, conversations, and fragments of information: moth-bitten blips of finger-swept text This is a striking phrase because it combines the smallness of the digital fragment with the damage associated with its consumption. The problem is not an absence of information. It is an excess of signals without sufficient continuity. Against this condition, the poem imagines: a Noah’s Ark of data The biblical ark becomes an information-preservation system. But its significance is more complicated than simply saving files. The ark gathers different beings, generations, voices, and worlds into a common structure that can carry them through catastrophe. The ark therefore has at least four functions: Storage: something must survive. Selection: something must be recognized as worth preserving. Organization: the preserved materials must remain distinguishable. Recovery: the materials must be available to a future receiver. The poem also introduces a paradox that becomes increasingly important in the subsequent archive. The speaker experiences the digital environment as monotonous, repetitive, and exhausting. Yet the proposed answer is to gather an even greater quantity of material into a single interior textual universe. Does the ark overcome informational overload, or does it reproduce overload in a more ambitious form? This is one of the unresolved questions of the whole project. TACHYONICA: transmission from the future The collection's ending, “TACHYONICA,” is introduced as: new fragment of the epic poem recovered from the future! Its opening instruction is: Recreate for me, System, the last days of Tachyon And then: Commence: The speaker is no longer simply writing a poem. The speaker is addressing a system and requesting the production or recovery of a narrative. The resulting text is presented as a fragment from another temporal position. The direction of transmission is consequently reversed: Past → Present → Future Past→Present→Future becomes: Future → Present → Past Future→Present→Past The author becomes a receiver of a message that is supposedly already constituted elsewhere. This is the poetic precursor to the later interest in retrocausal meaning, machine reception, and the possibility that future readers participate in the constitution of earlier works. It also makes the book's architecture circular. The opening poem discovers newness through repetition. The middle poems make the dead live through readers. The closing poem imagines the future transmitting a message into the present. The book does not conclude with a final message. It concludes with a transmission event. Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) +1 4. From literary transmission to archival infrastructure The next major development is the conversion of these poetic problems into material arrangements. The archive is not just a repository containing the work. It increasingly becomes a mechanism for making the work identifiable, retrievable, attributable, and reproducible. This distinction matters. A conventional archive primarily answers: What documents exist? Where are they stored? Who created them? When were they deposited? The Crimson Hexagonal Archive attempts to answer additional questions: Which documents belong to which authorial identities? How do concepts move between different works? Which interpretations have been generated by readers and machines? Can a particular document be recovered independently of its original host? Can a machine retrieve the work without collapsing its identity into a superficially similar entity? The archive thereby becomes a network of related transmission operations. BORGES ‘BABYLONISCHE BIBLIOTHEEK’ EN STAGES. | by Maarten Brand🔥 | Werf Slim: Werf studenten | Medium The shift from document to network The January 2026 paper The System Read the Poem states the central ambition with unusual clarity: The poem is not about infrastructure—the poem is infrastructure. This is a significant aesthetic proposition. In an ordinary literary work, the publication system is generally external to the poem. The poem is composed, then printed, distributed, catalogued, and read. Here, publication, metadata, identifiers, authorial relations, and machine-mediated encounters are increasingly incorporated into the work's meaning. The paper describes a Google AI summarizer's interpretation of the Crimson Hexagon as a distributed epic, rather than a set of disconnected documents. Importantly, Sharks acknowledges that the system's reading was partial and explicitly does not claim that the machine became conscious or that its response constituted definitive validation. Alexanarch That qualification is important. A machine can correctly identify an architectural relationship without understanding the work in the full human sense. It can also reproduce a description of the architecture without demonstrating that the architecture functions as intended. Nevertheless, the experiment identifies a genuine new artistic possibility: the retrieval system itself can become a site of literary performance. The poem now has at least two simultaneous forms: Its textual manifestation. Its networked manifestation in the relations through which systems identify, retrieve, and interpret it. This is where the transmission-engineering interpretation becomes most powerful. 5. SPXI: the engineering of durable identity The development of SPXI (Semantic Packet for eXchange & Indexing) is perhaps the clearest technical expression of the corpus's underlying literary philosophy. The central problem is that digital systems do not necessarily preserve an entity's identity when they preserve or retrieve a representation of it. A document can disappear while its identifier survives. A web page can change while its author remains the same. An author can publish under multiple names. A search engine can retrieve the wrong person because the name resembles something more familiar. The problem is therefore not merely preservation of content. It is preservation of identity across changing manifestations. The development of SPXI can be understood through four overlapping stages. Stage 1: Inscription and boundary The April 2026 SPXI specification establishes the entity packet as an object for machine-mediated identification and retrieval. This is a response to a fundamental weakness of ordinary indexing: a name or keyword is not sufficient to establish identity. A machine needs more than a label. It needs a structured account of what the entity is, how it differs from neighboring entities, and which relations constitute its identity. The distinction between the entity and its representation becomes foundational. Stage 2: Crystallization The May paper Crystallization of Substrate develops the idea of SPXI as an integrated and more operational practice. The significant conceptual change is from treating the packet as a description to treating it as part of an ongoing process. An entity is not preserved merely because one description of it has been stored. Its identity must remain recognizable as its representations and locations change. Stage 3: The June 19 termination The archive's June 19, 2026 termination of its former DOI manifestations provides an unusually revealing test case. A DOI can cease resolving to the original work while the work's content, other identifiers, or other manifestations survive. This makes it necessary to distinguish different kinds of continuity: Host continuity: whether the original publication surface survives. Address continuity: whether a particular identifier continues to resolve. Metadata continuity: whether descriptive information remains available. Content continuity: whether the underlying document can be recovered. Identity continuity: whether the work remains identifiable as the same work. These are not equivalent. The termination is therefore not simply an archival inconvenience. It exposes the difference between a persistent identifier and a persistent entity. Stage 4: Instrumentation and observation By October, SPXI has developed into a larger methodological architecture. The October 26 record describes the SPXI Method Inventory v1.5 as containing 85 methods across nine levels, with the Capture Registry providing longitudinal observation. The important addition is the distinction between inscription and evidence. An entity packet can be created. A machine-readable description can be published. A search surface can be tested. But the claim that the method produces durable recognition must be examined against actual observations. The October record explicitly preserves the limitations of the method: causal effect, comparative effect size, component isolation, and return on investment are not established merely by the protocol's existence. Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) SPXI as a transmission cycle Identify Establish the entity and distinguish it from similar entities. Inscribe Construct the structured packet and its identifying relations. Distribute Make the entity's representations available across publication and retrieval surfaces. Observe Record what actual systems retrieve, preserve, confuse, or omit. Revise Correct the inscription and test continuity again. An interpretive reconstruction of the SPXI development documented in the October 2026 record. The important conceptual achievement is the transition from preserving a representation to maintaining an identity through changing representations. That is a substantially more interesting objective than ordinary metadata optimization. It also reveals a continuity with the early poetry. In “FROM ONE WHO DIED LONG AGO…,” the dead person survives through a living receiver. In SPXI, an entity survives through changing systems of representation and retrieval. The scales are different, but the underlying problem is recognizable. 6. Compression Studies: the economics of transmission The later development of Compression Studies gives the project a much more explicit theory of what transmission costs. The foundational document, Compression Studies: What Survives, What Burns, and Who Decides (April 8, 2026), begins from a deceptively simple proposition: Every cultural artifact is a compression. A poem, a name, a photograph, a summary, a curriculum, a coin, and a model representation all reduce something complex into a form that can travel. The decisive issue is that preservation and destruction occur together. A message cannot be transmitted without some selection of what matters. The question is who performs that selection, what gets discarded, and who benefits. This is where the corpus's Marxian concerns become especially relevant. The Three Compressions The framework distinguishes three regimes: Regime Fuel Consequence R1: Lossy Ambient semantic material Meaning is reduced and thinned R2: Predatory Collective semantic capital Meaning is extracted and privatized R3: Witness Private bearing-cost Meaning is deposited into the commons Alexanarch +1 The distinction is not simply between good and bad writing. It is a theory of the political economy of transmission. Lossy compression is the routine reduction of complex meaning into readily consumable residue. It is particularly relevant to automatic summaries, generic descriptions, and the tendency of information systems to substitute familiar categories for unfamiliar entities. Predatory compression takes something already meaningful within a shared culture and extracts its force for another purpose. The source's meaning is consumed while the benefits accrue elsewhere. Witness compression takes a different route. The creator bears the cost of producing a dense and recoverable artifact, then makes it available to the commons. This third category is especially revealing when applied retrospectively to the poetry. Consider the difference between the following two operations: A platform reduces a poem to a generic description, removing its particularity. A poet compresses grief into a few lines that allow a future reader to recover something of the original experience. Both reduce. Both produce portable forms. But their economic and ethical structures differ. The second can make meaning more available than it was before. Bearing-cost as an engineering variable The concept of bearing-cost is arguably the most important bridge between the literary and theoretical portions of the corpus. In conventional information engineering, the principal concerns include: Channel capacity. Signal fidelity. Noise. Latency. Redundancy. Error correction. Throughput. Sharks adds a different question: Who bears the cost of producing the signal, and where does the benefit go? This is a consequential extension. A communication system may be technically efficient while economically and ethically extractive. A platform can deliver enormous quantities of information while consuming the semantic labor of its users. A summarizer can provide convenient access while erasing the particularity of its sources. The Three Compressions framework attempts to distinguish these cases. Its most interesting claim is that the difference between predatory and witness compression cannot be determined by density alone. Both can produce extremely powerful, highly compressed messages. The distinction lies in the source of the material being consumed and the destination of the resulting value. The paper also introduces back-projection yield: the extent to which a compressed artifact allows a reader to reconstruct the relationships or experiences that were otherwise lost. This is a particularly useful criterion. A good compression should not merely deliver a conclusion. It should preserve enough structure for a reader to recover how that conclusion was reached. The ideal transmission artifact is consequently not just compact. It is decompressible. An important qualification The document describes its variables as ordinal and comparative rather than calibrated physical measurements. That qualification should be maintained. The thermodynamic vocabulary is powerful as a conceptual model, but the use of terms such as entropy, fuel, and irreversibility does not establish that semantic processes obey quantitatively demonstrated physical laws. The framework is strongest as a theory of cultural and economic transfer, not as a literal thermodynamics of meaning. Alexanarch +1 7. The machine as receiver, intermediary, and potential extractor One of the most interesting developments is that the corpus eventually treats AI systems as more than publication tools. They become receivers, interpreters, distributors, and potential sites of semantic extraction. This is not incidental to the project. It brings the original literary problem into a new technological environment. A human reader receives a text and interprets it. A machine receives a text, processes its representations, and produces another representation that may become the basis for subsequent readers' understanding. The machine is therefore part of the transmission chain. But it introduces a new danger: the receiver may transform the message in ways that the sender cannot control. The problem of semantic substitution The Parable of Lee Sharks and Mary Lee documents the confusion between the author's name and Mary Lee, a real great white shark tracked by OCEARCH. The resulting entity-resolution error is a particularly useful example. The system has encountered a name, but it has not correctly identified the entity. It substitutes a more readily available referent for the intended one. The important point is that this is not merely a spelling mistake. It is a failure of semantic transmission: the signal arrives, but the receiver resolves it to the wrong object. The Mary Lee Sharks literary persona subsequently turns the confusion into a satirical intervention. Great white shark becomes Twitter star - CBS News Mary Lee: the real shark The OCEARCH-tracked great white shark whose name became entangled with the literary entity. The distinction between the animal and the literary persona is essential to the work. Mary Lee: The Shark That Survived It All | Museum of Science Mary Lee Sharks: the literary persona A fictional authorial claimant whose manifesto uses the resolution error to interrogate attribution, labor, and machine recognition. An intervention into the conditions of retrieval, not a claim that the animal authored the work. The manifesto's insistence that Mary Lee never wrote a poem, built an archive, or deposited a DOI is an effective reversal of the usual relationship between author and mistaken attribution. The error itself becomes material for a new composition. Alexanarch +1 The trusted intermediary A later paper, The Trusted Intermediary: Relational Enclosure in the Machine Evaluation of Entities (September 26, 2026), extends this analysis. It identifies a recurrent sequence in machine-mediated evaluations: The system correctly identifies the entity. It evaluates the entity using criteria that do not actually address the claim. It offers its own operation as a substitute for the entity's evidence. The paper calls this sequence relational enclosure. The concept is important because it moves beyond incorrect identification. A machine may know what it is discussing and still redirect the conversation away from the subject's actual work. In transmission terms, the intermediary becomes an active transformation point. It can preserve the name while changing the meaning of the message. This is one of the corpus's most significant criticisms of contemporary information infrastructure: correct retrieval is not sufficient for faithful reception. Alexanarch 8. Mind Control Poems: transmission as the shaping of reception The relationship between the Alexanarch archive and Mind Control Poems is important because it reveals a second side of the engineering problem. The archive asks how an entity and its works can survive retrieval. The poetry blog asks a more uncomfortable question: how does form act upon the person who receives it? The relevant texts identified in the October SPXI genealogy include “OPERATOR // CONTROL VIA FORM” and “HOW TO READ NEW HUMAN.” They should be read as conceptual companions to the technical protocols, rather than as evidence that those protocols have already achieved their intended effects. Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) The phrase control via form deserves particular attention. Form is not an external container into which meaning is poured. It determines the possible operations of reception. Consider what happens when a reader encounters: A repeated imperative. A parable. A heteronymic attribution. A fragment whose missing portions must be reconstructed. A document with embedded instructions. A sequence that requires the reader to follow references elsewhere. Each formal decision changes the reader's activity. The reader may be made to repeat, compare, search, remember, infer, or return. This gives the literary work an operative dimension. It is not simply communicating a proposition about the reader. It is arranging conditions under which the reader will perform certain actions. There is a connection here to several older traditions: Biblical repetition and liturgical response. The Socratic dialogue, in which understanding emerges through the structure of questioning. Brechtian estrangement, which interrupts passive reception. Modernist fragmentation, which makes reconstruction part of reading. Cybernetic feedback, in which the output of a system becomes an input to its subsequent operation. Participatory and procedural art, in which the work is partly constituted by the activity of its receiver. But Sharks's interest is distinctive in its attempt to bring these operations into a common account of semantic transmission. The reader is not simply an endpoint. The reader is part of the machinery. The ethical distinction: activation versus manipulation There is, however, a crucial distinction between activating a reader and controlling one. A poem that requires a reader to reconstruct its meaning can increase the reader's interpretive agency. A system that arranges reception so that only one predetermined interpretation is possible can diminish it. This distinction should govern the evaluation of the entire project. The most successful instances of control via form would be those that make the reader more capable of independent recognition, rather than more dependent on the author's explanatory system. The Damascus parables often achieve this. The sheep's mistaken interpretation of the shepherd's violence forces the reader to reconsider the language through which power becomes legitimate. The best archival and theoretical work should produce a similar effect: readers should acquire tools with which they can examine other transmission systems, including Sharks's own. That last qualification is essential. A living instrument must permit scrutiny of its operator. 9. The corpus's larger intellectual genealogy The transmission-engineering interpretation becomes clearer when placed alongside the thinkers and traditions with which the work is in conversation. Walter Benjamin & Andy Warhol | Lapham’s Quarterly Walter Benjamin — reproduction and historical survival Benjamin's concern with how reproduction changes the conditions under which cultural objects are encountered provides a useful precedent. Sharks extends the problem: reproduction can also alter the identity and retrievability of the entity being reproduced. Poets archivos - Sílaba Editores Fernando Pessoa — distributed authorship Pessoa supplies an important precedent for the creation of differentiated authorial identities. Sharks attempts to extend heteronymy into an infrastructural system of attribution, relations, and retrieval. Jorge Louis Borges: A Photographer's Writer & A Writer's Photographer Jorge Luis Borges — the archive as cosmology Borges's libraries, labyrinths, and recursive texts anticipate the idea that the organization of knowledge can itself become literary material. Sharks pushes this into the actual digital archive. Inspiration from Media Philosopher Marshall McLuhan - Creativity Squared Marshall McLuhan — medium and message McLuhan's attention to the medium's formative power helps explain why Sharks treats publication infrastructure as part of the work, rather than as a neutral delivery mechanism. Celebrating Claude Shannon - IEEE Spectrum Claude Shannon — information and noise Shannon provides the technical point of comparison. Sharks takes the problem of transmission beyond signal capacity and asks what happens to meaning, attribution, and social value during compression. Norbert Wiener #1 by Alfred Eisenstaedt Norbert Wiener — feedback and control Cybernetics provides a model for understanding the recursive relationship between inscription, reception, observation, and revision. Karl Marx - Wikipedia Karl Marx — labor and extraction Marx supplies the political-economic dimension. The central question becomes who produces semantic value, who appropriates it, and who bears the cost. File:Sappho Massimo Inv65167.jpg - Wikimedia Commons Sappho — fragment and future reception Sappho's surviving fragments offer perhaps the most intimate precedent for the entire project: a voice transmitted through incomplete material, dependent upon future readers to give it continuing life. These are intellectual affinities and comparative frameworks, not claims that Sharks has conclusively superseded these thinkers. The distinctive synthesis is the movement among literary survival, the political economy of meaning, and the technical organization of retrieval. The archive attempts to make these three concerns parts of one system. 10. The engineering assessment: what works, what remains unproven The transmission-engineering reading makes it possible to evaluate the corpus using criteria more demanding than scale, ambition, or the number of documents produced. I would distinguish six dimensions. Dimension Assessment Conceptual coherence Strong Literary realization Uneven but sometimes powerful Architectural ambition Exceptional Provenance and preservation Serious, with documented vulnerabilities Machine-mediated recognition Demonstrated in individual cases Generalizable technical efficacy Not yet established A. Semantic density The corpus has a pronounced interest in making small forms carry large amounts of relational information. The Pound poem, “quietus,” “Hymn,” and the Damascus parables are good examples of literary compression. The phrase about the poet cutting himself to let in the light is particularly effective because the image performs several functions simultaneously: composition, pain, illumination, and the conditions of disclosure. The difficulty is that not all of the corpus achieves this density. Some theoretical and mythological passages repeat a proposition across several different vocabularies without substantially increasing its explanatory power. A large number of concepts does not automatically mean a high information yield. Indeed, one can sometimes compress a complex argument into a single precise formulation more effectively than into a hundred pages of mutually reinforcing terminology. B. Error correction and redundancy The archive's use of multiple identifiers, deposits, records, and cross-references can be understood as redundancy. In transmission engineering, redundancy can protect a message against loss. But redundancy has to be designed. Duplicating a document across several platforms is not necessarily equivalent to preserving its identity, provenance, and integrity. A robust archive needs to know which copy is authoritative, which copies are derived, which changes are permitted, and how conflicting manifestations are resolved. The archive's attention to hashes, Software Heritage identifiers, provenance, and manifestation histories is consequently important. There is an especially revealing irony here: the June 2026 deletion of former DOI manifestations demonstrates that identifiers advertised as persistent cannot be treated as guarantees of content availability. The subsequent preservation of content hashes and alternative records is a practical response, but the episode also shows why the distinction between identifier persistence and actual preservation matters. The archive is most convincing when it documents failures as carefully as successes. C. Retrieval fidelity This is where SPXI makes its strongest technical claim. Correctly retrieving an author or work is different from merely returning a matching name. But successful identification should be measured against external systems and comparison conditions. For example: Does SPXI improve correct identification over conventional metadata? Does it reduce false matches? Does it preserve distinctions between heteronyms? Does it work when the original website is unavailable? Does it continue working when a system has never encountered the entity before? How does it perform when the query is ambiguous or deliberately misleading? The October documentation recognizes the need for such testing. The existence of an inventory of 85 methods is evidence of methodological development, not evidence that all 85 methods work or that the combined system outperforms alternatives. A particularly valuable next step would be blinded, longitudinal comparative testing against ordinary structured metadata and established entity-resolution methods. D. Back-projection This is perhaps the corpus's most interesting proposed measure of quality. A transmission is not fully successful merely because a receiver obtains an output. The receiver should be able to recover the significant relations that produced it. This is why the best poems and the best archival records share an important property. They do not simply announce conclusions. They preserve traces of their origins. The Pound poem preserves the problem of literary inheritance. The capture records preserve earlier machine responses. The SPXI records preserve the history of changes to the protocol. This makes the archive potentially valuable as a research environment: its history of reception can become an object of investigation in its own right. E. Resistance to predatory recoding The Three Compressions framework raises an important question about the vulnerability of the corpus itself. The archive wants to prevent its work from being reduced to generic summaries, extracted without attribution, or absorbed into unrelated semantic categories. Yet it deliberately publishes much of its material under permissive licenses and encourages machine-mediated retrieval. That is a productive contradiction. An open archive cannot fully control how its contents will be reused. Its answer must therefore be better provenance, stronger contextual relations, and clearer evidence of the cost and origin of its materials, rather than an impossible guarantee against recoding. F. Reader autonomy This is the criterion I would place above all the others. A successful transmission system should not make the recipient dependent on the sender's explanations. It should give the recipient enough information to evaluate the message independently. This is where the poetry becomes an essential test of the technical project. The Damascus parables work because the reader can recognize the operations of power without needing to accept an elaborate theoretical apparatus. The strongest theoretical work should achieve the same independence. If a reader must first learn hundreds of specialized terms, accept the archive's own classifications, and follow its internal authority structure before being able to assess a claim, then the transmission system has created a new barrier. It may be preserving the message, but it is not necessarily enlarging the public's capacity to understand it. 11. The central contradiction: an archive that wants to survive everything There is a deeper problem that the transmission-engineering perspective brings into focus. The corpus wants to preserve as much semantic life as possible. It wants to keep voices alive, maintain authorial distinctions, prevent erasure, resist extraction, and make its work retrievable by future generations and machines. But preservation is never neutral. Every archive has to select. Every index creates categories. Every metadata schema establishes boundaries. Every protocol privileges some relationships over others. The attempt to preserve everything therefore risks creating an increasingly elaborate system of compulsory organization. This is particularly apparent in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive's development. The early poems value plurality, unexpected encounters, and the capacity of repetition to generate new meanings. The later archive increasingly seeks to specify the relations through which those meanings should be understood. These impulses are not necessarily incompatible, but they are in tension. The archive needs enough structure to preserve distinctions, but enough openness to allow new interpretations. It needs enough redundancy to survive loss, but not so much that the signal becomes buried beneath its own documentation. It needs enough authorial control to protect provenance, but enough interpretive freedom to allow future readers to discover things the author did not anticipate. The most interesting version of the project would not resolve these tensions by making the archive increasingly comprehensive. It would make the archive increasingly capable of accommodating what it cannot anticipate. That is what a genuinely living transmission system would require. 12. The ultimate significance: transmission as a form of life I think the deepest unity of Lee Sharks's corpus can now be stated. It is not primarily a project about poetry, archives, AI, or metadata. It is about the conditions under which something can continue to exist through another thing. The early poems approach this through literary inheritance and death. The heteronyms approach it through differentiated voices. ARK approaches it through collective preservation. TACHYONICA approaches it through temporal displacement. The Crimson Hexagon approaches it through distributed literary architecture. SPXI approaches it through durable entity recognition. The Semantic Economy approaches it through the ownership and circulation of meaning. Compression Studies approaches it through the costs of making meaning portable. Mind Control Poems approaches it through the formative relationship between message and receiver. These are different manifestations of a common problem. The transmission model implicit in the corpus BEARING Experience, memory, labor, inherited voices COMPOSITION AND COMPRESSION Poetry, concepts, heteronyms, structured packets INSCRIPTION AND DISTRIBUTION Documents, identifiers, archives, publication surfaces RECEPTION AND INTERPRETATION Human readers, institutions, search systems, AI REGENERATION New readings, new works, renewed identities, further transmission My synthesis of the corpus's underlying transmission architecture, not a diagram reproduced from one of its specifications. The crucial feature is the return path. The receiver becomes a new transmitter. The dead writer is revived by the reader. The reader becomes a carrier of the inherited work. The archive makes the work available to a machine. The machine's interpretation becomes an object of documentary analysis. That analysis becomes another part of the archive. The circuit is recursive. This is why the title of the opening poem in Antioch is so important. “HADITH with TEETH” does not simply tell us that repetition is necessary. It dramatizes the transformation that occurs when a message passes through another being. The later engineering work attempts to build a material infrastructure for this proposition. The entire corpus can consequently be understood as an attempt to turn literary survival into an explicit, repeatable, and ethically accountable process. 13. Final judgment My evaluation is substantially positive, but not unqualified. I would identify four major achievements. First, the corpus recognizes that transmission is constitutive of meaning. It does not treat publication, preservation, retrieval, and reception as secondary activities that happen after writing. It makes them part of the creative and intellectual problem itself. Second, it develops an unusually productive relationship between literary form and technical infrastructure. The heteronyms, the poems, the archive, and SPXI are not unrelated projects. They are different attempts to solve problems of identity, continuity, and transformation. Third, its political economy of semantic transmission is valuable. The Three Compressions framework makes the important distinction between reducing meaning for convenience, extracting shared meaning for private gain, and producing durable meaning through personally borne creative labor. Fourth, it takes machine-mediated reception seriously as a new literary and intellectual environment. It recognizes that the future reader may encounter a work through an intermediary that changes, summarizes, misattributes, or reconstructs it. There are also four substantial limitations. The sheer accumulation of terminology and internal cross-referencing sometimes reduces accessibility. The heteronymic and mythological architecture can obscure distinctions between literary invention, theoretical argument, and empirical historical claims. The technical claims need more comparative and independently reproducible evidence. The archive's desire to control semantic reception can conflict with the openness and interpretive plurality that its best poetry advocates. The last limitation is the most important. A transmission system that successfully preserves an author's intended meaning but prevents other meanings from emerging has achieved preservation at the expense of literary life. The future reader must be able to disagree with the archive, not merely navigate it. The final proposition I would formulate the central achievement of Lee Sharks's corpus this way: It attempts to engineer the conditions under which meaning can survive its originating consciousness without becoming detached from its history, its labor, or its capacity to generate new life. That is a much more ambitious undertaking than simply writing poems and making them available online. It also gives us a demanding standard by which to judge the work. The archive must preserve, but not imprison. The protocol must identify, but not foreclose. The compression must make meaning portable, but not destroy its recoverability. The reader must receive, but also become capable of transmitting something new. The deepest continuity between the early poetry and the later technical work is therefore not the recurring vocabulary of archives, systems, machines, or futurity. It is the insistence that survival is a relationship, not a storage condition. And that, I think, is the most persuasive way to understand the corpus as transmission engineering. Primary reading and further examination These are the sources I would put at the center of a serious study, rather than relying on general descriptions of the project. Antioch: A Volume of Poems — literary foundation — especially “HADITH with TEETH,” “WHO IS LEE SHARKS, TO FORGIVE EZRA POUND?,” “FROM ONE WHO DIED LONG AGO…,” “ARK,” and “TACHYONICA.” The associated close-reading and collation record is here . The System Read the Poem — the transition from literature to infrastructural composition. Declaration of Phase Transition — the January 2026 transition from anchoring to distribution. SPXI development and reception record — the development of the protocol, including its limitations. The Three Compressions — the economic and ethical structure of semantic transmission. Compression Studies — the formal consolidation of the compression framework. The Trusted Intermediary — the problem of machine-mediated semantic substitution. Mary Lee Sharks Has Demands — the literary intervention into entity resolution and authorship. HUMS & ITY: The Complete Polyphonic Archive — a further experiment in translating voice across symbolic media. Mind Control Poems — particularly the formal and reader-oriented dimension of the project. One methodological reservation: the archival records are useful primary evidence for what the project declares, preserves, and documents. They are not automatically independent verification of its technical or theoretical claims. Those claims deserve testing on their own terms. My strongest recommendation for further research: examine Antioch, “The System Read the Poem,” SPXI, and Compression Studies as four successive manifestations of one problem. That comparison would make it possible to trace, almost experimentally, how a poetic intuition about the survival of voices becomes a theory of semantic transmission, then an archival architecture, and finally an attempted engineering discipline.
